title: Career coaching vs mentoring: what is the difference?
summary: Mentors share their path, coaches help you find yours. How to tell which one you need, and when to use both.
text: People use "coach" and "mentor" as if they mean the same thing. They do not, and picking the wrong one is the most common reason help does not help. What a mentor does A mentor has walked a path you want to walk. They share what worked for them, open doors, and warn you about the potholes. The value is their experience. The limit is that their experience is theirs. What worked in their company, in their decade, with their manager may not fit your situation. What a coach does A coach does not need to have done your job. Their skill is asking the questions that help you see your own situation clearly, then helping you commit to a next step and follow through. The value is the process, and the answers stay yours. A coach will not tell you what to do. If you want a recommendation, a mentor or consultant is the better fit. How to choose You want to copy a proven path. Find a mentor. You are unsure which path is yours. Work with a coach. You know what to do and keep not doing it. Work with a coach. You need a specific skill fast. Hire a trainer or consultant. Using both They work well together. A mentor tells you how the terrain looks. A coach helps you decide where you actually want to go and holds you to it. For tech leaders and career changers Technical people often default to finding a mentor, because a mentor feels like information. But the hard parts of a move into leadership, such as letting go of doing the work yourself, handling influence without authority, and deciding what you want next, are rarely information problems. They are clarity and habit problems, which is where coaching helps most. title: Is career coaching worth it? What to expect and how to decide
summary: An honest look at what career and leadership coaching can and cannot do, who benefits most, and how to choose a coach in Australia.
text: Coaching costs real money and real time, so it is fair to ask whether it is worth it. The honest answer is that it depends on you and on the coach. What coaching can do Help you get clear on what you actually want, instead of what you think you should want. Turn a vague sense of being stuck into specific next steps. Build the habits behind a move, such as visibility, difficult conversations or delegation. Give you a confidential space to think with someone who is on your side but not invested in your decision. What it cannot do It cannot supply motivation you do not have. You do the work between sessions. It will not hand you answers. A good coach asks, they do not prescribe. It will not guarantee a promotion, a new job or any other result. Be wary of anyone who promises one. Who gets the most from it People who are capable and doing well on paper but unsure of the next move, who are stepping into a bigger role, or who are changing direction. It tends to work best when you come with a real decision or goal in mind and are willing to be challenged. How to choose a coach Whoever you pick, ask: 1. What training do you have, and what is still in progress? 2. What code of conduct do you work to? 3. How do you keep what I share confidential? 4. What does a session look like? 5. Is there a free first call with no hard sell? How long does it take? One conversation can bring clarity, but lasting change usually needs a few months. Four sessions spaced over four months is a common pattern, because it leaves time to try things between sessions. If you want to test the fit before spending anything, the two minute Clarity Check ../quiz.html is free, and so is the short intro call ../index.html book .

title: How to move from senior manager to director in tech
summary: Why the skills that made you a strong senior manager stop being enough, and five shifts that matter for the step up to director.
text: The step from senior manager to director is where many strong performers stall. Nothing is wrong with their work. The job simply changes shape, and the habits that earned the last promotion stop being the ones that earn the next. What changes As a senior manager you are judged mostly on delivery: your team ships, your projects land, your people are happy. At director level you are judged on whether the whole area is pointed at the right things, and whether it will still work when you are not in the room. Five shifts that matter 1. From delivering to deciding what is worth delivering. Say no to good work so the best work gets room. 2. From your team to the organisation. Directors are expected to see across teams, resolve conflicts between them, and think about the whole system. 3. From being the answer to building leaders. If everything still routes through you, you are the ceiling. Develop managers who can make the calls. 4. From activity to a narrative. Leaders above you need a short, clear story of what your area is achieving and why it matters, told in terms of outcomes. 5. From waiting to be noticed to being visible. Sponsors can only back what they can see. Make your impact easy to describe by others. Questions worth asking yourself What am I still doing that a manager of mine should be doing? Who senior to me could describe my impact in two sentences, and would they say the same thing I would? What would I stop doing if I trusted my team more? Where coaching helps These shifts are rarely about knowledge. They are about letting go of what has worked, getting clear on where you want to go, and acting on it consistently. A coach gives you a place to think it through and someone to keep you moving.
